standard.title: Organisational responses to improve human wellbeing
standard.description: responses of international and national government and non-government organisations to improve human wellbeing in Australia, within India and another country in the Pacific
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand causes and consequences of wellbeing variation at global scale (AC9HG10K05), within a country in Asia (AC9HG10K06), and within Australia including for First Nations Australians (AC9HG10K07). They are positioned to evaluate organisational responses against the causes identified in those earlier standards.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and explain responses of government and non-government organisations to improve human wellbeing in Australia, India and a Pacific country, evaluating programs against their objectives and outcomes.

nodes.label: Types of organisations and their approaches
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the types of organisations that respond to wellbeing issues — international (e.g. UN agencies), national government (e.g. AusAID equivalents), and non-government (e.g. World Vision, Red Cross) — and explain how their mandates and approaches differ.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the role of at least two different types of organisation (e.g. one government, one NGO) and explain how their approach to improving wellbeing differs.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe the different mandates, funding sources, target populations and methods of international government organisations, national government programs and NGOs; explain how the type of organisation shapes the approach taken.
wider: Examine tensions between different organisational types — for example, where government programs and NGO programs in the same country or community have conflicting priorities or methods
Investigate how organisations coordinate (or fail to coordinate) in complex humanitarian or development contexts — examining the UN coordination architecture for a specific crisis
Research the growth of social enterprise and community-led organisations as a third approach between government and NGO models, with examples from Australia's First Nations sector

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate government programs and NGOs, or assume all aid organisations do the same thing. An explicit framework distinguishing types by mandate, funding, accountability and target population prevents blurring that undermines evaluation in Node 2.

success_criteria: Students distinguish between at least two types of organisations (government, NGO, international) by mandate and approach
Students explain how an organisation's type shapes what it can and cannot do to improve wellbeing

nodes.label: Programs and their objectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the objectives and outcomes of specific programs to reduce wellbeing inequality in Australia, India and a Pacific country.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one specific program in at least one country context, identifying its objectives and what it targets.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain programs in each of the three mandated contexts (Australia — including First Nations wellbeing; India or regional inequalities; Pacific country); describe program objectives, target populations and intended outcomes for each.
wider: Research how AusAID's objectives and methods evolved over time and compare its approach to wellbeing improvement with that of an equivalent bilateral aid agency (e.g. USAID, DFID/FCDO)
Investigate the evidence base for a specific NGO program (e.g. World Vision's Zonal Health Program, Red Cross WASH programs) by examining reported outcomes data
Examine community-proposed ways to improve First Nations wellbeing in Australia and compare these with government-initiated programs, identifying points of alignment and divergence

response_modes.reason: The descriptor requires three country contexts — students need genuine engagement with programs in each, not a single case study applied across all three. The teaching signal is to ensure coverage of all three contexts with sufficient specificity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Program comparison across Australia, India and a Pacific country reveals how the same organisational approaches operate very differently in different development contexts — a rich comparative case set that builds evaluative sophistication.
success_criteria: Students identify at least one specific program in each of the three contexts (Australia, India/regional, Pacific) and describe its objectives
Students explain what each program targets and who the intended beneficiaries are

nodes.label: Evaluating program effectiveness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of programs to improve wellbeing, connecting program outcomes to the causes of wellbeing inequality identified in earlier standards.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate the effectiveness of one program against its stated objectives, identifying at least one strength and one limitation.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate programs in terms of whether they address the identified causes of wellbeing inequality; consider whether outcomes match objectives; acknowledge limitations of evaluation data (selectivity, short-term framing, aid dependency risks).
wider: Apply a consistent evaluation framework (e.g. OECD-DAC criteria: relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability) to compare two programs in the same region
Investigate a program that has been independently evaluated and compare self-reported outcomes with external evaluation findings — examining the gap and what produces it
Explore critiques of aid and development programs more broadly — evaluating whether program approaches address structural causes of inequality or focus on symptoms

response_modes.reason: Program evaluation integrates understanding of wellbeing causes (K05-K07) with program analysis — a good evaluation requires students to connect the program's approach to the actual drivers of the wellbeing issue it addresses. The teaching signal is to make this connection explicit rather than treating evaluation as stand-alone.

success_criteria: Students evaluate a program against its stated objectives, identifying at least one strength and one limitation with evidence
Students connect the program's approach to at least one identified cause of wellbeing inequality, explaining whether or not the program addresses that cause
